produced_by: Prompt 83 (dashboard data export). Presentation simplification of reports/modeling/ALL_LEGS_SUMMARY.md (Prompt 81) -- no number here is re-derived; each carries its source.

comparability.rule: Never sort or rank all six legs on one axis. Binary legs are scored with PR-AUC (a yes/no separation metric); continuous legs are scored with R-squared (a how-close-is-the-number metric). Comparing a PR-AUC of 0.43 with an R-squared of 0.45 is a category error, not a finding. Even the four continuous legs split into two sub-families (hurdle vs two-stage xT) with different target distributions and architectures, so compare within a group only.

groups.title: Will a shot follow?
groups.plain_description: Probability that the attacking team takes a shot within 10 seconds of the moment being scored.
groups.headline_metric_plain: How well the model picks out the moments that really did lead to a shot (0 to 1, higher is better). A model guessing at random scores roughly the share of moments that lead to a shot.

groups.title: How dangerous is the shot that follows?
groups.plain_description: Expected shot quality (xG) in the next 10 seconds, built as P(shot) x expected xG given a shot, reusing that side's own shot-probability model.
groups.headline_metric_plain: Share of the variation in what actually happened that the model explains (0 = no better than a flat average, 1 = perfect).

groups.title: How much threat did the defence take away?
groups.plain_description: Expected change in expected-threat (xT) around the moment, from a two-stage model: P(threat changes at all) x expected change given it does.
groups.headline_metric_plain: Share of the variation in the actual threat change that the model explains (0 = no better than a flat average, 1 = perfect).

legs.question: After a tackle, interception, pressure or other on-ball defensive action, how likely is a shot within 10 seconds?
legs.model_family_plain: Gradient boosting, with calibration so the probabilities can be read at face value
legs.one_liner: Promoted only after a slice-level calibration check overruled the uncalibrated version's better-looking headline numbers.

legs.question: Given where one off-ball defender is standing when the attacker plays the ball, how likely is a shot within 10 seconds?
legs.model_family_plain: Gradient boosting, with calibration so the probabilities can be read at face value
legs.one_liner: Promoted with one weak spot flagged rather than hidden: defenders the pipeline could not assign a role to (a thin slice).
legs.source_note: ALL_LEGS_SUMMARY.md section 2 describes a 3rd-decimal discrepancy (CSV 0.210773 vs doc 0.2162). Re-checked in Prompt 83: 0.210773 is the UNCALIBRATED p1e_gradient_boosting row of that CSV; the calibrated reference row is 0.21619, matching the doc. There is no discrepancy.

legs.question: After an on-ball defensive action, how much shot quality (xG) should we expect in the next 10 seconds?
legs.model_family_plain: Random forest for shot quality, combined with the active shot-risk model
legs.one_liner: A real but modest end-to-end gain: most moments never lead to a shot, so the shot-probability half dominates the product.

legs.question: Given one off-ball defender's position, how much shot quality (xG) should we expect in the next 10 seconds?
legs.model_family_plain: Simple log-normal linear model (the starting baseline, never beaten), combined with the passive shot-risk model

baseline_to_reference.source: ALL_LEGS_SUMMARY.md section 4 (Rung 0 is the reference model)

legs.reference_confirmed_current: Confirmed in Prompt 83 against MODELLING_CLOSEOUT.md section 2 and ALL_LEGS_SUMMARY.md section 2: d1_lognormal_glm is the standing reference (d1d_random_forest failed its gate, p=0.576).
legs.one_liner: Three different upgrades were tried and none beat the simple starting model -- reported as the finding, not hidden.

legs.question: How much does an on-ball defensive action change the attacking team's expected threat?
legs.model_family_plain: Two-stage random forest (does threat change? then by how much?)
legs.one_liner: About 3x the explained variance of its starting model, and the win held equally in both tournaments.

legs.question: How much does an off-ball defender's position change the attacking team's expected threat?
legs.model_family_plain: Two-stage random forest (does threat change? then by how much?)
legs.one_liner: About 8x the explained variance of its starting model, and it removed a systematic over-prediction the linear models could not fix.

active_vs_passive.headline: There is no project-wide 'passive improves more' (or 'active improves more') story -- the answer flips by target family.

by_family.plain: Active gained more in absolute terms, passive more in relative terms.
Active improved; passive did not improve at all.
Passive improved far more -- but only in this family.

cross_leg_pattern.headline: Random forest won 3 of the 6 legs -- and was tried on all 6.
cross_leg_pattern.detail: It won the three continuous/two-stage legs with the most data. On the other three it lost for leg-specific reasons: worse calibration (active shot risk, where it was run as a diagnostic), a failed significance test (passive shot risk, p=0.275), and a failed significance test on a smaller, noisier sample (passive shot danger, p=0.576).
